SERIAL RAPE PROSECUTORS

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
In a rising tide of violent sex crime, the women of the Joburg DPP take us behind the scenes of their work and lives to show what it takes to put serial rapists behind bars.

Unique Selling Point:
We have the unique opportunity to spend time on the job with 4 senior advocates...ordinary women -- wives, mothers, sisters -- who take on extraordinary evil, every day at the office of the Johannesburg Directorate for Public Prosecutions, as prosecutors of some of the country's most heinous serial rapists and murderers.

I believe the women's personal stories provide a way of addressing the current narratives and trends around violence against women and children in SA in a way that is constructive, hopeful and inspiring.

In March this year, one of two serial rapists dubbed the "Balaclava Rapists" had his face covered with a scarf in court when he was convicted on 53 charges of rape, compelled rape, assault, sexual assault and robbery with aggravating circumstances. His victims had been aged between 13 and 38. He had started his spree in 2007 and was arrested in 2015 (Carte B instrumental in solving the case after the community complained to us...then a SAPS unit was set up) and the case eventually landed in the pile of dockets on the DPP assignments desk .

Senior State Advocate Michelle Bayat, a Randburg wife and mother of twin boys in her 30s was assigned the case -- to run it simultaneously with a heavy caseload of economic crimes. What haunts her is the total lack of remorse in the first convicted rapists' eyes. Since running the case, she even finds it hard to pass by women walking on the street without worrying for their safety. This case -- and the many other less famous ones like this -- has changed her.

This coming week Michelle will be presenting arguments in aggravation of sentencing of a second man who was charged. The men have been linked to the crime by DNA evidence, but the second accused steadfastly denies guilt.

Michelle draws much courage from her colleagues (who've become friends) in the DPP.

-- Zarina Peck (38) is a petite woman who was a senior advocate for only a couple of years when she got the case of the "Caretaker Rapist" -- a caretaker at a school, where he used his access to kids to groom more than 40, from ages 13 to 16, using pornography and raped them. He had carried on for years before the crime was discovered in 2015.

Zarina prosecuted the man on 33 dockets; some of the children had moved on and would not be deposed. Zarina speaks with passion of what it takes to win a child's trust -- she has 3 of her own at home. She had serious nightmares throughout the case, but despite the NPA's well-intended wellness programme and counselling offered, she had no time in the midst of her heavy caseload to attend sessions. In the end she turned to her Muslim faith, prayer and her colleagues to process the trauma.

-- In her fifties, Phakanyisa Marasela is the oldest of the women and a quiet source of strength in the team. She feels she has a special insight into the psyche of women, which compelled her to complete a law degree after stating her career as a court translator in the 1980s. She worked her way up through the courts until she landed in the high-rise home of the DPP opposite the Joburg High Court ten years ago.

Phakanyisa wants to share her struggle in getting a conviction in the case of two accused rapists who raped 6 women and murdered 5 before they were caught. To this day, Phakanyisa is driven by the brutal crime scene photos in her docket, and she's been struggling since 2012 to get justice for the woman (all of whom have since passed away). Accused Nr. 1 confessed and has already been sentenced -- the second remains in custody and the trial is set down for January 2018. All this time, Phakanyisa has been in contact with the children and families of the victims, and want to bring them closure.

-- Ten years ago, Nerissa Muller begged the Joburg DPP for a job when she found herself as a public defender unable to defend "one more scumbag". Now she's become the "Mama" of al the kids that seemed to land in her caseload of late -- in particular the case of a man who raped 38 children (who could be traced) from Limpopo to Thembisa.

Colleagues honour Nerissa's skill with children and in particular disabled kids -- she's found rapists target disabled kids precisely because they "won't talk" or possibly even understand what's happening to them...but Nerissa will spend days before trial, even weekends to play with the kids in the room where they're to testify, making it safe for them...and making it possible to nail the criminals.

The work of these prosecutors is nothing like television court dramas. They have no interns, candidate attorneys or secretaries to make copies of documents or help them feed restless, traumatised children who have to spend long days in court. They do it all themselves -- and they want to do it all with excellence, so that none of the criminals they prosecute will get away on stupid technicalities.

They've given us access to follow them around for a couple of days at the office, and in court, and have welcomed us into their homes -- (with the exception of their own children, who will not be part of any filming).

They all speak extremely eloquently and their communications officer and managers have agreed to accommodate us.

Press Release:


There’s a rising tide of violent sex crimes in South Africa and often it takes exceptional legal expertise and a special way with people to put serial rapists and murderers behind bars. With a long list of convictions between them, Carte Blanche meets four extraordinary advocates – all women - who take on some of the country’s most dangerous sex offenders in the courtroom.

Script:


VO: From all corners of Greater Johannesburg, four state advocates make their way to the city’s courts daily to lead the charge against serial rapists.

CLAIRE MAWISA LINK: Far too often we see headlines screaming of sexual crimes committed against women and children. The worst of the worst are serial offenders.

VO: Nerissa Muller is one of about 3000 state prosecutors countrywide. She started out defending perpetrators for Legal Aid but her heart lay with victims.

ADV. NERISSA MULLER: We work with people that are devastated, people that’s lives have been torn apart.

VO: Zarina Peck had her sights set on law from a very early age.

ADV. ZARINA PECK: This will be my fourteenth year in this job. It’s escalating, rape and murders and especially on our children. The victims are becoming younger.

VO: Pakanyiswa Marasela chose this path, because she felt there were things women who survived rape would best share with a woman.

ADV. PAKANYISWA MARASELA: In our job it’s about helping people to see that justice is done. You must forget about yourself.

VO: Michelle Bayat scored a big blow this month for the numerous victims of Josias Mkansi, one of the two so-called balaclava rapists who operated for a decade in Alexandra. Carte Blanche helped crack the case by making the link between numerous open dockets at the local police station after activists complained to us. A task team was formed in 2015 and the cases were linked through DNA evidence.

ADV. MICHELLE BAYAT: Once a victim makes a statement and reports it to the police station, most of these lay victims think that is the end of the matter. They do not realise that when we arrest a suspect the matter goes to court and I can’t prove my case without their evidence.

VO: Mkansi was handed 14 life sentences plus 185 years in jail for attacking young couples and raping the women.

ADV. MICHELLE BAYAT: I had an agonising time contacting victims. The under-aged victims ... their parents refused to let them come, even for a consultation. So I was worried about how they would fare in court.

VO: Mkansi first asked how old some of the girls were before raping them. It’s hard enough for adult survivors to face the trauma -- but it takes special commitment to earn the trust of children and guide them through the court process.

CLAIRE MAWISA: I heard you have a tattoo … could you explain that?

ADV. NERISSA MULLER: Yes... after Khoza serial matter I wanted something to remind me of the case and the emotions that I’ve gone through...and also remember the children.

VO: In 2016, Peter Dashboy Khoza received 28 life sentences and another 538 years behind bars for kidnapping and assaulting 45 children and raping 28 of them from Limpopo to Soweto over 6 years. The children were aged between 7 and 14.

ADV. NERISSA MULLER: Khoza was a special creature. He targeted children in groups. He would see three, four sometimes six girls playing in a park and then he will approach them and start talking to them and make them to trust him… And so I got the tattoo of the outline of a tulip on my arm. I also have a wrinkle to remember the Khoza case. I didn’t have it before the Khoza case.

CLAIRE MAWISA: It forever changed you, then.

ADV. NERISSA MULLER: It made me grow, it also brought me a lot closer to God. Those times where I just felt so alone, all these little eyes looking at me to help them. Don’t think that when I started the Khoza case I knew everything about children -- they taught me a lot about life as well.

VO: Prof Gerard Labuschagne is a former police officer and lent his expertise as one of the country’s top crime profilers to Nerissa and Michelle’s cases.

PROF. GERARD LABUSCHAGNE, FORENSIC PSYCHOLOGIST: If you caught every serial rapist after the first rape, you wouldn’t have the opportunity to become a serial. So if we’re having massive amounts of serial rapes, getting up to 10, 15, 20 victims, it means we’re not properly, effectively policing these crimes.

CLAIRE MAWISA: When we hear of all these gruesome details happening to children, how does that affect you just as a woman?

ADV. NERISSA MULLER: Well, I’m not going to try to be tough, because even if you have your prosecutor gown on, these things affect you. We had a child that…she was so traumatised when she had to identify the photo of the accused that she took the earphones off…that she used to testify and just threw it against the window. We had some that scream. You experience all this trauma. Remember we only have it secondary -- they have it first degree.

VO: Though it’s been two years since Zarina secured a conviction in the case of a school soccer coach who groomed kids with pornography from the age of seven and repeatedly raped them, she grapples with how events marked the victims.

ADV. ZARINA PECK: The youngest victim was seven and he had been raped and groomed from that age up until the accused was arrested four years later. And this boy walks into my office, dressed like a girl. And you know what he says to me? I don’t know who I am... Did the accused groom me this way? You know what, I’ll never forget that case. And I said to him, you be who you are. You be who you are. You ask me, what makes me go on? It was hope. It was a bittersweet conviction.

CLAIRE MAWISA LINK: The details of every victim’s story live on with the prosecutor long after the case is done and are often visible in their own private spaces.

ADV. PAKANYISWA MARASELA: I wake up, even it is 12 o’clock, immediately I wake up and go and check if all the doors are locked. Even if I arrive home in the afternoon, I will check if there is something funny outside there at the gate. Because I must look for strange things, because you’ll never know.

VO: Pakanyiswa is a single mom and pillar of strength for her extended family. Her 24-year old son Lungile was one when she began the arduous studies that would take her from court interpreter to advocate. She’s working to prosecute a serial rapist and murderer who lured victims with the promise of jobs.

ADV. PAKANYISWA MARASELA: There were photos in these dockets, Claire. Some of the ligatures around their necks were still there. You could see that now this body has got maggots, it is decomposed. I didn’t sleep that night.

CLAIRE MAWISA: What motivates you to keep going on a case that has been running now for years?

ADV. PAKANYISWA MARASELA: The families of the victims.

VO: This job with its long days of painstaking paperwork and gut-wrenching consultations is far removed from the LA Law fantasies of Michelle’s youth.

ADV. MICHELLE BAYAT: So if I’m driving down a street and it’s a lonely street and I see a single female and then a few metres away I would see a male walking, I mean innocently, the thought…the first thought that comes to my mind is that he’s going to attack her. I feel bad for feeling that way, but I see it all the time. I read it in the dockets. This job makes you very suspicious about your surroundings...and also very protective of my family members as well. They do get a bit irritated with me, but sorry...

PROF. GERARD LABUSCHAGNE, FORENSIC PSYCHOLOGIST: Even if we feel we are coping effectively, you start to realise the level of tension you are operating on, and stress.

ADV. ZARINA PECK: I think I’ve metamorphosed into this type of a person that is extremely paranoid... it tends to eat you up inside. So you need coping mechanisms. So when I get home, it’s faith, family, my parents.

CLAIRE MAWISA LINK: Experts say it is generally accepted that only one in every nine rapes are reported, and less than 10% of the cases reported eventually make it to court. So, while sex crimes stats soar, that’s really only a fraction of the true picture.

JUDGE INGRID OPPERMAN: The evidence points to the conclusion that women’s right to give or withhold consent to sexual intercourse is one of the most commonly violated of all human rights in South Africa.

ADV. MICHELLE BAYAT: It makes me happy that I’ve made a small difference in this victim’s life. And if, it may not give her total closure, but it helps in that healing process.

VO: According to crime statistics just released, nearly 40 000 rape cases were reported in the last year. In 9% of cases, the victims were younger than 10 years old. In the last three years, the Johannesburg High Court’s state advocates have prosecuted 56 serial rapists with close to 1300 charges against them.

PROF. GERARD LABUSCHAGNE, FORENSIC PSYCHOLOGIST: From crime scene to courtroom, you really have to have people who know what they’re doing. And recently, the minister of police released a serial policy that will hopefully be implemented soon that says you have to consolidate these cases under trained people. I don’t think we’ve ever lost a serial prosecution in South African history -- the final crux is that prosecutor right at the end who puts that case together in court.

ADV. MICHELLE BAYAT: The courts are dishing out heavy, lengthy terms of imprisonment. But we put away five perpetrators and there’s another five perpetrators out there.

ADV. PAKANYISWA MARASELA: As I’m sitting here now, yesterday I received a box with 11 dockets, rape and robbery.

CLAIRE MAWISA LINK: Advances in science make it easier to convict serial offenders, like the Balaclava Rapists, who were linked to the crimes through DNA. But this DNA would be nothing without the commitment of the professionals who use it as a powerful tool.

ADV. ZARINA PECK: Those victims are the heroes. They get into that box. They’re basically saying, I’m not going to allow it anymore.

ADV. NERISSA MULLER: There is a lot of people that is invested in these serials and I believe that we are going to win this battle one of these days. One serial rapist by one serial rapist, but we’re going to win them, definitely.


​PROMOS
10 secs
In the rising tide of violent sex crime -- who do we rely on to put the worst offenders behind bars? Meet some extraordinary prosecutors of serial rapists.

15 secs
Die-hard prosecutors of Joburg’s high courts fight the growing scourge of serial rape, with victims ever younger...
ADV. ZARINA PECK: Those victims are the heroes. They get into that box. They’re basically saying, I’m not going to allow it anymore.

Meet the dedicated prosecutors of the Joburg High court who are honing the skill of prosecuting serial rapists to a fine art.

PAKANYISWA MARASELA: I wake up, even it is 12 o’clock, immediately I wake up and go and check if all the doors are locked. Even if I arrive home in the afternoon, I will check if there is something funny outside there at the gate. Because I must look for strange things, because you’ll never know. VO: Pakanyiswa is a single mom and pillar of strength for her extended family. Her 24-year old son Lungile was one when she began the arduous studies that would take her from court interpreter to advocate. She’s working to prosecute a serial rapist and murderer who lured victims with the promise of jobs. ADV. PAKANYISWA MARASELA: There were photos in these dockets, Claire. Some of the ligatures around their necks were still there. You could see that now this body has got maggots, it is decomposed. I didn’t sleep that night. CLAIRE MAWISA: What motivates you to keep going on a case that has been running now for years? ADV. PAKANYISWA MARASELA: The families of the victims. VO: This job with its long days of painstaking paperwork and gut-wrenching consultations is far removed from the LA Law fantasies of Michelle’s youth. ADV. MICHELLE BAYAT: So if I’m driving down a street and it’s a lonely street and I see a single female and then a few metres away I would see a male walking, I mean innocently, the thought…the first thought that comes to my mind is that he’s going to attack her. I feel bad for feeling that way, but I see it all the time. I read it in the dockets. This job makes you very suspicious about your surroundings...and also very protective of my family members as well. They do get a bit irritated with me, but sorry... PROF. GERARD LABUSCHAGNE, FORENSIC PSYCHOLOGIST: Even if we feel we are coping effectively, you start to realise the level of tension you are operating on, and stress. ADV. ZARINA PECK: I think I’ve metamorphosed into this type of a person that is extremely paranoid... it tends to eat you up inside. So you need coping mechanisms. So when I get home, it’s faith, family, my parents. CLAIRE MAWISA LINK: Experts say it is generally accepted that only one in every nine rapes are reported, and less than 10% of the cases reported eventually make it to court. So, while sex crimes stats soar, that’s really only a fraction of the true picture. JUDGE INGRID OPPERMAN: The evidence points to the conclusion that women’s right to give or withhold consent to sexual intercourse is one of the most commonly violated of all human rights in South Africa. ADV. MICHELLE BAYAT: It makes me happy that I’ve made a small difference in this victim’s life. And if, it may not give her total closure, but it helps in that healing process. VO: According to crime statistics just released, nearly 40 000 rape cases were reported in the last year. In 9% of cases, the victims were younger than 10 years old. In the last three years, the Johannesburg High Court’s state advocates have prosecuted 56 serial rapists with close to 1300 charges against them. PROF. GERARD LABUSCHAGNE, FORENSIC PSYCHOLOGIST: From crime scene to courtroom, you really have to have people who know what they’re doing. And recently, the minister of police released a serial policy that will hopefully be implemented soon that says you have to consolidate these cases under trained people. I don’t think we’ve ever lost a serial prosecution in South African history -- the final crux is that prosecutor right at the end who puts that case together in court. ADV. MICHELLE BAYAT: The courts are dishing out heavy, lengthy terms of imprisonment. But we put away five perpetrators and there’s another five perpetrators out there. ADV. PAKANYISWA MARASELA: As I’m sitting here now, yesterday I received a box with 11 dockets, rape and robbery. CLAIRE MAWISA LINK: Advances in science make it easier to convict serial offenders, like the Balaclava Rapists, who were linked to the crimes through DNA. But this DNA would be nothing without the commitment of the professionals who use it as a powerful tool. ADV. ZARINA PECK: Those victims are the heroes. They get into that box. They’re basically saying, I’m not going to allow it anymore. ADV. NERISSA MULLER: There is a lot of people that is invested in these serials and I believe that we are going to win this battle one of these days. One serial rapist by one serial rapist, but we’re going to win them, definitely. ​PROMOS 10 secs In the rising tide of violent sex crime -- who do we rely on to put the worst offenders behind bars? Meet some extraordinary prosecutors of serial rapists. 15 secs Die-hard prosecutors of Joburg’s high courts fight the growing scourge of serial rape, with victims ever younger... ADV. ZARINA PECK: Those victims are the heroes. They get into that box. They’re basically saying, I’m not going to allow it anymore. 15 secs ADV. PAKANYISWA MARASELA: In our job it’s about helping people to see that justice is done. Forget about yourself. Meet the dedicated prosecutors of the Joburg High court who are honing the skill of prosecuting serial rapists to a fine art.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): In a rising tide of violent sex crime, the women of the Joburg DPP take us behind the scenes of their work and lives to show what it takes to put serial rapists behind bars.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We have the unique opportunity to spend time on the job with 4 senior advocates...ordinary women -- wives, mothers, sisters -- who take on extraordinary evil, every day at the office of the Johannesburg Directorate for Public Prosecutions, as prosecutors of some of the country's most heinous serial rapists and murderers. I believe the women's personal stories provide a way of addressing the current narratives and trends around violence against women and children in SA in a way that is constructive, hopeful and inspiring. In March this year, one of two serial rapists dubbed the "Balaclava Rapists" had his face covered with a scarf in court when he was convicted on 53 charges of rape, compelled rape, assault, sexual assault and robbery with aggravating circumstances. His victims had been aged between 13 and 38. He had started his spree in 2007 and was arrested in 2015 (Carte B instrumental in solving the case after the community complained to us...then a SAPS unit was set up) and the case eventually landed in the pile of dockets on the DPP assignments desk . Senior State Advocate Michelle Bayat, a Randburg wife and mother of twin boys in her 30s was assigned the case -- to run it simultaneously with a heavy caseload of economic crimes. What haunts her is the total lack of remorse in the first convicted rapists' eyes. Since running the case, she even finds it hard to pass by women walking on the street without worrying for their safety. This case -- and the many other less famous ones like this -- has changed her. This coming week Michelle will be presenting arguments in aggravation of sentencing of a second man who was charged. The men have been linked to the crime by DNA evidence, but the second accused steadfastly denies guilt. Michelle draws much courage from her colleagues (who've become friends) in the DPP. -- Zarina Peck (38) is a petite woman who was a senior advocate for only a couple of years when she got the case of the "Caretaker Rapist" -- a caretaker at a school, where he used his access to kids to groom more than 40, from ages 13 to 16, using pornography and raped them. He had carried on for years before the crime was discovered in 2015. Zarina prosecuted the man on 33 dockets; some of the children had moved on and would not be deposed. Zarina speaks with passion of what it takes to win a child's trust -- she has 3 of her own at home. She had serious nightmares throughout the case, but despite the NPA's well-intended wellness programme and counselling offered, she had no time in the midst of her heavy caseload to attend sessions. In the end she turned to her Muslim faith, prayer and her colleagues to process the trauma. -- In her fifties, Phakanyisa Marasela is the oldest of the women and a quiet source of strength in the team. She feels she has a special insight into the psyche of women, which compelled her to complete a law degree after stating her career as a court translator in the 1980s. She worked her way up through the courts until she landed in the high-rise home of the DPP opposite the Joburg High Court ten years ago. Phakanyisa wants to share her struggle in getting a conviction in the case of two accused rapists who raped 6 women and murdered 5 before they were caught. To this day, Phakanyisa is driven by the brutal crime scene photos in her docket, and she's been struggling since 2012 to get justice for the woman (all of whom have since passed away). Accused Nr. 1 confessed and has already been sentenced -- the second remains in custody and the trial is set down for January 2018. All this time, Phakanyisa has been in contact with the children and families of the victims, and want to bring them closure. -- Ten years ago, Nerissa Muller begged the Joburg DPP for a job when she found herself as a public defender unable to defend "one more scumbag". Now she's become the "Mama" of al the kids that seemed to land in her caseload of late -- in particular the case of a man who raped 38 children (who could be traced) from Limpopo to Thembisa. Colleagues honour Nerissa's skill with children and in particular disabled kids -- she's found rapists target disabled kids precisely because they "won't talk" or possibly even understand what's happening to them...but Nerissa will spend days before trial, even weekends to play with the kids in the room where they're to testify, making it safe for them...and making it possible to nail the criminals. The work of these prosecutors is nothing like television court dramas. They have no interns, candidate attorneys or secretaries to make copies of documents or help them feed restless, traumatised children who have to spend long days in court. They do it all themselves -- and they want to do it all with excellence, so that none of the criminals they prosecute will get away on stupid technicalities. They've given us access to follow them around for a couple of days at the office, and in court, and have welcomed us into their homes -- (with the exception of their own children, who will not be part of any filming). They all speak extremely eloquently and their communications officer and managers have agreed to accommodate us.
